Issued at 201 AM EDT Fri Oct 30 2026

             -----------Synoptic Overview-----------

Florida's weather is currently influenced by a broad area of
above-normal H5 heights, with a ridge axis from the Mississippi
Valley to the Yucatan Peninsula. A modest pressure gradient exists
over Florida, between lower pressures over the Greater Antilles
and high pressure over the Tennessee Valley. A polar jet streak
will pass from the Great Lakes to New England over the next 36
hours, sending another strong continental high (1030-1035 hPa)
toward the Northeast U.S. This is expected to tighten the pressure
gradient over Florida as we push into the weekend, maintaining
fresh onshore flow in the boundary layer.

Upstream, subtropical jet energy is gathering from the Chihuahuan
Desert to the Eastern Pacific.  A piece of this energy is forecast
to stream eastward, arriving over the state on Sunday. Upper jet
diffluence is likely to increase, particularly from Sunday into
early Monday. Simultaneously, PWATs are forecast to exceed 201% 
of normal, increasing the potential for a period of enhanced 
moisture transport and low-level convergence. Global ensembles 
then slowly move this disturbance into the Atlantic by around 
Tuesday.

Behind this feature, shortwave ridging should move over the state
from Tuesday into Wednesday. Confidence then begins to decrease
late next week. Guidance has hastened the arrival of the next
mid-latitude trough, with it most likely reaching the Deep South by
early Thursday. With another subtropical jet disturbance emerging
from the Four Corners late next week, a more progressive outcome 
appears plausible.

Within this progressive, largely zonal pattern, a cold front 
should weaken as it approaches Central Florida around Thursday. 
In fact, H85 (5 kft) temperatures are forecast to remain near to
above normal into next weekend. However, modified continental 
air is expected to lower humidity values behind the front.

             -------Sensible Weather & Impacts-------

Today - Saturday...

No significant weather changes are anticipated as we close out
the work week and enter the first half of the weekend. Breezy
northeast winds today will turn easterly and increase a bit on
Saturday, with peak gusts of 20-30 mph in most cases. Sufficient
moisture will remain in place for 30-50% coverage of onshore-moving
showers. The greatest coverage should be near the coast, especially
the Treasure Coast. Lightning chances remain low, around 20%.

Hazardous conditions will persist at our beaches and for mariners.
Expect 4-6 ft breaking waves in the surf zone and numerous,
deadly rip currents. Displaced sandbars and beach erosion will
will pose additional risks for beach-goers. Please remain out
of the ocean! The highest tides will occur around midday. Minor
to moderate coastal flooding is still a concern today along the
entire coast. By Saturday, we expect peak tide levels to lessen
slightly for all but the southern Treasure Coast. At least minor
tidal flooding is expected to continue into Saturday, especially
south of St. Lucie Inlet.

Highs will remain in the low to mid 80s, with nighttime lows
staying warm in the low to mid 70s courtesy of onshore winds.

Sunday - Monday...

The most active weather of the next seven days is expected Sunday
into Monday. The combination of subtropical jet stream energy,
ample moisture, and persistent onshore flow appears capable of
producing bands of heavy rainfall and isolated storms. While
frictional convergence will be maximized along the coast, locally
excessive rainfall cannot be ruled out over the interior of east
central Florida.

Average rainfall tallies of 1-3" are forecast during this period,
with a 5-10% chance of storm total amounts exceeding 5 inches. 
Due to recent rainfall, our FLASH-CREST soil saturation model 
indicates that areas from far southern Brevard to Martin counties 
are most vulnerable to flash flooding.

Breezy east-northeast flow will continue off the Atlantic, with a
few gusts of 20-30 mph. Any storms that develop may produce locally
stronger gusts. The weather will not be nice to beach-goers, but
those venturing out should keep in mind that hazardous conditions
will continue. 5-6 ft surf should persist along with a high risk
of rip currents. Highs will be modulated slightly into the upper
70s and low 80s by the clouds and rain.

Tuesday - next Friday...

Heavy rain potential abates beginning Tuesday, but 30-50% shower
chances linger for the middle of the week as sufficient moisture
remains in place. More intervals of sun should return, and winds
become noticeably lighter by Wednesday. This will allow high temps
to warm back into the low and mid 80s for the middle of the week.

A cold front is forecast to reach Central Florida around
Thursday. Indications are that the front will be weakening on
approach, but it may squeeze out a band of showers and a few
storms. Severe weather potential currently appears limited.
